title: Die casting
wiki_lead:
Die casting is a metal casting process that is characterized by forcing molten metal under high pressure into a mold cavity. The mold cavity is created using two hardened tool steel dies which have been machined into shape and work similarly to an injection mold during the process. Most die castings are made from non-ferrous metals, specifically zinc, copper, aluminium, magnesium, lead, pewter, and tin-based alloys. Depending on the type of metal being cast, a hot- or cold-chamber machine is used.
The casting equipment and the metal dies represent large capital costs and this tends to limit the process to high-volume production. Manufacture of parts using die casting is relatively simple, involving only four main steps, which keeps the incremental cost per item low. It is especially suited for a large quantity of small- to medium-sized castings, which is why die casting produces more castings than any other casting process. Die castings are characterized by a very good surface finish (by casting standards) and dimensional consistency.

History
Die casting equipment was invented in 1838 for the purpose of producing movable type for the printing industry. The first die casting-related patent was granted in 1849 for a small hand-operated machine for the purpose of mechanized printing type production. In 1885 Ottmar Mergenthaler invented the Linotype machine, which cast an entire line of type as a single unit, using a die casting process. It nearly completely replaced setting type by hand in the publishing industry. The Soss die-casting machine, manufactured in Brooklyn, NY, was the first machine to be sold in the open market in North America. Other applications grew rapidly, with die casting facilitating the growth of consumer goods, and appliances, by greatly reducing the production cost of intricate parts in high volumes. In 1966, General Motors released the Acurad process.


Cast metal
The main die casting alloys are: zinc, aluminium, magnesium, copper, lead, and tin; although uncommon, ferrous die casting is also possible. Specific die casting alloys include: zinc aluminium; aluminium to, e.g. The Aluminum Association (AA) standards: AA 380, AA 384, AA 386, AA 390; and AZ91D magnesium. The following is a summary of the advantages of each alloy:

Zinc: the easiest metal to cast; high ductility; high impact strength; easily plated; economical for small parts; promotes long die life.
Aluminium: lightweight; high dimensional stability for very complex shapes and thin walls; good corrosion resistance; good mechanical properties; high thermal and electrical conductivity; retains strength at moderately high temperatures.
Magnesium: the easiest metal to machine; excellent strength-to-weight ratio; lightest alloy commonly die cast.
Copper: high hardness; high corrosion resistance; highest mechanical properties of alloys die cast; excellent wear resistance; excellent dimensional stability; strength approaching that of steel parts.
Silicon tombac: high-strength alloy made of copper, zinc and silicon. Often used as an alternative for investment cast steel parts.
Lead and tin: high density; extremely close dimensional accuracy; used for special forms of corrosion resistance. Such alloys are not used in foodservice applications for public health reasons. Type metal, an alloy of lead, tin and antimony (with sometimes traces of copper), is used for casting hand-set type in letterpress printing and hot foil blocking. Traditionally cast in hand jerk moulds, now predominantly die cast after the industrialisation of the type foundries. Around 1900 the slug casting machines came onto the market and added further automation, with sometimes dozens of casting machines at one newspaper office.

grok_lead: Die casting is a precision manufacturing process in which molten metal is injected under high pressure into a reusable steel mold, called a die, to form complex, net-shape or near-net-shape components with tight dimensional tolerances and smooth surface finishes. This method excels in high-volume production, enabling the creation of intricate geometries, thin walls, and features like threads or holes that minimize the need for secondary machining. Primarily suited for non-ferrous metals, die casting produces durable parts with enhanced mechanical properties, recyclability, and cost efficiency for mass production. The origins of die casting trace back to the early 19th century, when it was developed to produce movable type for the printing industry using low-melting alloys like lead and tin. The process was invented in 1838, with the first patent granted in 1849, marking the shift from manual to mechanized processes, with significant advancements in the 1880s, including the Linotype machine for automated typesetting with molten lead alloys. By the 20th century, the process had evolved into modern variants, including high-pressure, low-pressure, and vacuum-assisted techniques, driven by industrial demands in automotive and aerospace sectors. Common materials for die casting include aluminum alloys (such as A380 and 360), which offer lightweight strength and corrosion resistance; zinc alloys (like Zamak No. 3), prized for precision and thin sections; magnesium alloys (e.g., AZ91D) for superior strength-to-weight ratios; and copper-based alloys for high conductivity applications. Among these materials, aluminum alloys remain one of the most popular choices for industrial die casting due to their excellent performance in structural integrity and versatility across automotive, aerospace, and precision manufacturing sectors. Lead and tin alloys are used rarely due to their lower mechanical properties. These materials solidify rapidly under pressure, resulting in parts with minimal porosity and high integrity. Die casting finds extensive applications in industries requiring robust, complex components, including automotive parts like engine brackets, transmission housings, and wheels; electronics enclosures and heat sinks; consumer products such as power tool housings and faucet fittings; and industrial equipment gears and structural elements. Its key advantages encompass rapid cycle times for high productivity, material efficiency with low scrap rates, excellent surface quality that reduces finishing needs, and the integration of multiple features to lower assembly costsâmaking it a cornerstone of efficient, scalable manufacturing. However, it involves high initial tooling costs, limiting its suitability for low-volume runs.
